title: Can Kafka and Solace be used together: yes, many companies use Kafka as the durable system of record for long-term event retention and replay, and Solace for dynamic event distribution and selective routing to consumers: they solve different problems and are often complementary?
shortTitle: Can Kafka and Solace be used together, and why are they often complementary?
keyPoints: Kafka and Solace are frequently used together because they solve different problems and complement each other.
Kafka serves as the durable system of record with long-term retention, replay, and stream processing.
Solace serves as the dynamic distribution layer with broker-native hierarchical routing and low-latency fan-out.
A common pattern bridges them so events flow through Solace for live routing and into Kafka for durable storage.
Pick one system of record (usually Kafka) so if the two diverge you know which is authoritative.
The bridge is a first-class component: a stalled bridge silently breaks either durability or live delivery.
Events that match no live Solace subscription are still persisted to Kafka, keeping the durable record complete.

s1_definition.oneliner: Solace routes live events flexibly to the right consumers now; Kafka durably stores every event for replay later; and bridging them gives you both.
s1_definition.profdef:
Yes, Kafka and Solace are frequently used together because they solve different problems and complement each other.

- **Kafka as system of record** – a partitioned, append-only log that retains events for the long term and supports deterministic replay, event sourcing, and stream processing.
- **Solace as distribution layer** – a broker-native hierarchical router that delivers precisely filtered slices to many heterogeneous consumers with low latency and no topic creation.
- **Bridge** – a connector or adapter that moves events between the two systems, ensuring every routed event also has a durable home and every stored event can be distributed.
- **System of record** – one authoritative source of truth (usually Kafka) so if the two diverge you know which to trust.
- **Complementary design** – each tool handles what its model does best, avoiding the pitfalls of forcing one into the other's role.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, Solace is the smart mail room that instantly sorts each incoming transaction alert to exactly the desks that asked for that kind of alert, as desks keep changing their requests. Kafka is the permanent records vault where a copy of every alert is filed in order and kept for years, so auditors can replay the entire history whenever they need. The mail room makes sure the right person gets the right alert now; the vault makes sure nothing is ever lost and everything can be reconstructed later. A courier (the bridge) makes sure every alert that passes through the mail room also gets filed in the vault.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, Kafka and Solace are very commonly used together, and the reason is that they solve different problems and complement each other rather than compete. Kafka is the durable system of record: a partitioned log that retains events for years and supports offset-based replay, event sourcing, and stream processing. Solace is the dynamic distribution layer: a hierarchical router that delivers precisely filtered slices to many consumers with low latency and without creating new topics.

The way they fit together is a bridge. A transaction event is published once, Solace routes it live to exactly the desks whose wildcard subscriptions match, and the bridge captures the same event into a Kafka topic retained for years. Live consumers get only their slice without topic proliferation, while Kafka keeps the complete, ordered, replayable record for compliance and analytics. Even events that match no live subscription are still persisted to Kafka because the bridge subscribes to everything.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj ran exactly this architecture. Trading desks wanted diverse, frequently changing slices of the live transaction feed, so Solace handled the selective routing. Compliance needed every transaction stored durably for seven years and replayable to rebuild the ledger, so a bridge captured every event into Kafka as the authoritative system of record. The bridge was monitored as first-class infrastructure with alerts on throughput, errors, and lag.

Remember one sentence: Solace makes sure the right desk gets the right event now, Kafka makes sure nothing is ever lost and the whole history can be replayed later, and a monitored bridge connects them.
